findings.finding: “We partly replicated the planning findings of Kupzyk (2011)” opens the abstract, describes four original findings, and is explained by the adjusted power comparisons, one-cluster threshold moves and extreme-setting disagreement.
“We partly replicated Kupzyk’s headline findings” precedes the fresh-sample scope and the signed losses, threshold match count and empirical-below-exemplary counts.

The main text defines each power method, then gives the empirical question, comparator and matched pairs without requiring an earlier draft. Repository disagreement identifiers follow descriptions sufficient to understand the findings.

Routes R and S distinguish numerical regeneration from source measurements, with a separate report rebuild. Wrapped paths and the disagreement tag isolated at the head of page 3 are minor layout roughness. No clipping or unreadable main text on pages 1–12.

The original loss ordering, lowest-ICC peak, planning cluster penalty and majority empirical-below-exemplary result are identified. Both retention of the ordering and the three threshold shifts are visible. The abstract adds the adjusted 54-cell empirical agreement and Appendix D divergence without replacing the headline.

Independently recomputed the Table 1 paired means and the R final-grid aggregates. In both, allocation is largest, 15% dropout is next, both size effects are below 1 pp, and all five losses peak at ICC .05. The printed prose’s stronger monotonic claim is contradicted by the published and R skewed-size aggregates, as stated here.

Kupzyk pp. 106–107 gives the full-grid count of 41 and only 51 pairs can be read from the figures. Counting the R signed gaps gives 40; the manuscript keeps the two source evidentiary routes separate.

Checked mapped ch1, rq1–rq4, hypothesis-order, thresholds and practical-verdict. Three power approaches and matched loss estimands are explicit, the source prediction and findings are distinguished, and the threshold table independently yields 51 exact crossings and the three stated shifts.

Checked oversample and ch3. Six participant-loss cases clear .80, and the 19-cluster source value is outside the central mask interval. The separate twelve observation-loss rows and completer arithmetic are represented. The crossed factors and reported population model appear here and on page 4.

Checked appendix-a, appendix-b, formula-od, formula-bw, ch4 and initial-empirical. R generator and optimizer checks and three covariance implementations are distinguished. The formulaic table supports the even and odd crossings and baseline between–within power. The initial power comparison separates the two ordinary exceedances from the adjusted family.

findings.location: Section 4, empirical versus exemplary paragraph; Chapter V interpretation

findings.location: Sections 5 and 6, with baseline Section 5 beginning on page 5
findings.finding: Checked null-baseline, null-extreme, ch2 and precision. The original and rerun D.1 rates, narrower Serlin classification, both D.2 gaps and diagnostic df sensitivity, two software discrepancies and G*Power agreement, and the independent precision illustration are present.

Reviewed mapped limits 0–2. Missing historical software, streams and masks bound replay, the three occluded markers do not silently become observations, and the original realized-design and R mask-mean estimands are kept distinct. Appendix C diagnostic precision is explicitly conditional on a proxy for unreported source error.

Mapped limits 3 and 7 are retained: .88187 falls below the central interval, the adverse mask is only a feasibility diagnostic, and available-observation power is separate from completers-only arithmetic.

Mapped limits 4, 5 and 8 are retained: a smaller effective D.2 df is compatible but historical use is unresolved, the original Optimal Design software inputs and Figure 4 streams are unavailable, and observed-count df is a reconstruction assumption.
Mapped limit 6 restricts the ranking to the tested Gaussian four-occasion design and dropout mechanism, and a numerical paired example illustrates that the size contrasts vary by setting.
The scientific partial verdict is stated separately from the inability to replay the source state, and the magnitude labels are explicitly point estimates rather than equivalence.

The assertion that the two D.1 gaps preserve the practical classifications is ambiguous against the manuscript’s explicit change in point classifications for the narrower Serlin interval on pp. 5–6. Name the broad Bradley interval as the scope of preservation and keep the distinct narrower conclusion.

The author-year attribution and the reference match the wrapper and title page of the archived dissertation. Its own abstract supports the substantive attrition/allocation versus size result and lowest-ICC pattern. Printed pp. 97–98 and 106–107 support the additional threshold and empirical-versus-exemplary attributions. The source title, institution, document type and persistent record are verified against the first two physical pages and the page 12 reference.

findings.location: Table 1, signed effects and comparison note
findings.finding: The five main signed losses independently recompute from printed p. 92 Table 1 and the final-grid paired data. At the .001 pp tolerance their magnitude labels are smaller, larger, larger, smaller and smaller. Both operands are positive in every row. The .001 pp tolerance is two weighted half-units at .001 pp source precision, derived from five decimals on the original probability scale.

For ICC the .05 minus .15 high-dropout loss is 3.0366667 versus 3.0621750 pp; four half-units yield .002 pp. Eight versus seven extra clusters and 41−27 versus 40−27 cells use .5 integer comparison precision. Signed direction remains the same for each. The note labels the comparisons point estimates and explicitly separates equivalence, reading error, mask variation and Monte Carlo uncertainty.
Published 1.3 pp agrees with the source prose on printed p. 93, and Ours 1.27 pp agrees with the aggregate of the 18 matched final R pairs, 1.274814 pp.

Published gives a qualitative reduction even though printed p. 93 reports a 4.4 pp mean loss. Ours likewise omits the 4.471858 pp observed loss from the paired R data. Put the quantitative finding in each of the finding cells, with the signed columns retained separately.
Published 6.4 pp matches the p. 95 average across 27 50/50 to 70/30 matched settings; Ours 6.44 pp matches the final R aggregate of 6.443263 pp.
Published .45 pp is the p. 95 mean against equal size; Ours .44 pp matches the 18-pair R aggregate .438215 pp.
Published .85 pp is the pp. 95–96 mean against equal size; Ours .78 pp matches the 18-pair R aggregate .778279 pp.

Both cells correctly describe the .05 peak, but identical text omits the qualification material to the row’s partial verdict. Published p. 96 asserts decreasing loss with rising ICC, while its own Tables 1 and 4 show a skewed-size rise from .10 to .15; the R reconstruction independently shows the same exception. Represent the source’s statement and the rerun’s observed exception in their respective cells, retaining the selected 15% quantitative contrast.

The published p. 97 Table 5 and prose support up to eight extra over the between–within reference. The threshold-comparison data give at most seven extra for the mean crossings, with 32 versus the 25-cluster reference at the most extreme setting.

Published 41/54 is explicitly reported on p. 106 for the initial grid. Ours 40/54 is the independent count of negative R empirical-minus-exemplary values. The cells report the raw counts rather than the centered signed effect.
